validity.researcher_notes: The recorded LengthKnown=860 mi is demonstrably a STALE, HISTORICAL figure, not the pipeline's current length. Two independent sources state explicitly that 860 miles was the ORIGINAL 1929 construction: encyclopedia.com ('Interstate's [PEPL's original 1929 name] original network consisted of an 860-mile line that supplied the Midwest with gas from the southwest Kansas and Texas panhandle') and Wikipedia ('When Panhandle Eastern Pipe Line incorporated in 1929 as Interstate Pipe Company, the entity started with 860 miles of line'). Both then describe major subsequent growth (1989 Texas Eastern merger, multiple owner changes, and per the SEC 10-K, an internal build-out to four parallel large-diameter lines). PEPL's own FY2021 10-K (the SEC's most recent, filed 2022-02-18) states the CURRENT system in two different ways in the same paragraph: (1) 'The Company's [Panhandle's] transmission system consists of FOUR large diameter pipelines extending approximately 1,300 miles from producing areas in the Anadarko Basin of Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas through Missouri, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and into Michigan' (i.e. a ~1,300-mile ROUTE corridor now carrying 4 parallel strings, not 1); and (2) the summary statistics table: 'Approximate Miles of Pipelines -- Panhandle 6,000' (i.e. ~6,000 total miles of PIPE when all 4 parallel strings + laterals/loops are summed -- roughly consistent with 4 x 1,300 route-miles plus loops). Wikipedia independently corroborates the larger figure: 'Panhandle Eastern Pipe Line Company, LP is an approximately 6,300-mile natural gas interstate pipeline system.' So there are two internally-consistent CURRENT candidates -- ~1,300 mi (route/corridor) or ~6,000-6,300 mi (total installed pipe, the figure PEPL itself reports as 'Miles of Pipelines' and that Wikipedia echoes) -- and NEITHER is 860. I propose 6,000 mi as the primary candidate because it is literally PEPL's own answer to 'how many miles of pipeline,' it is corroborated by Wikipedia's independent 6,300-mi figure, and it is the same style of system-total figure this tracker already carries on peer multi-line network rows in this same batch (P0168 CIG 6,920 mi, P0222 NGPL 9,100 mi) -- but I did not silently overwrite the cell because GEM's segment-vs-network convention for a single-row system like this one is a judgment call for a human, not a mechanical fix: if this row is meant to represent one logical route/corridor rather than total installed pipe, ~1,300 mi (also SEC-10-K-sourced) would be the better number. Either way, 860 is wrong for a currently-operating characterization of the line and should not stand uncorrected. Proposed refs (both verified, both name Panhandle Eastern Pipe Line specifically): https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/76063/000007606322000010/pepl-20211231.htm and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panhandle_Eastern.

No source found that dates a distinct 'proposal' separate from the 1929 incorporation/construction of the original line (already sourced on Start [ref]). For a pipeline whose founding predates FERC's modern certificate process by decades, a discrete proposal date is unlikely to be independently documented. Searched: the SEC 10-Ks (no project-proposal language, only current operations), encyclopedia.com and Wikipedia corporate histories (give incorporation/construction context, not a separate proposal date), and a general web search for 1928-1930 construction history (surfaced a Rice University Woodson Research Center archive description of a 'Panhandle Eastern Pipeline history, growth story, pipeline construction; 1930-1967' collection and a paywalled Time magazine 1930s article, neither of which I could open/verify the actual text of, so neither is cited).

Same search as Proposal [ref] above. Sources place incorporation in 1929 and describe the original network as already built/operating by then ('the entity started with 860 miles of line' at incorporation), which argues construction substantially preceded or coincided with the 1929 incorporation date rather than following it as a distinct later year -- but I could not verify a specific construction-start year/month distinct from 1929 on any page I could actually read in full (a Rice University archive finding aid and a paywalled Time archive piece were located but not opened/verified, so not cited). Left blank rather than inferring a number from an unverified lead.

No operating-pressure figure found in the SEC 10-Ks (they report capacity, mileage and financials, not MAOP), Wikipedia, or encyclopedia.com. This kind of engineering detail typically lives in a FERC facility docket or PHMSA filing rather than corporate disclosures; did not locate a specific citable docket for it in the time available.

Confirmed via web search of Federal Register FERC notices that individual Panhandle segments/loops carry DIFFERENT diameters (a Parke County, Indiana loop upsizing 20-inch to 36-inch; a Marion/Boone/Hamilton County, Indiana loop upsizing 24-inch to 30-inch; various 24-42in ranges cited across expansion-project summaries) -- consistent with this being a large multi-segment, multi-vintage system (SEC 10-K: 'four large diameter pipelines') with no single system-wide diameter to report. Left blank rather than picking one segment's diameter to represent the whole row, consistent with the aggregate-vs-segment caution in the brief.

fills.researcher_notes: The schema note for FuelSource wants a named field/plant/facility, not a bare commodity type. 'Anadarko Basin' is the specific named producing region PEPL's own 10-K identifies as the line's supply source -- basin-level rather than a single named field (no single field/plant name was found in any source), so flagging that granularity gap for a human to accept-or-refine rather than defaulting to something vaguer. Tier medium (one primary source, no second independent source located for this specific basin attribution in the time available -- Wikipedia and encyclopedia.com describe the supply region more loosely as 'southwest Kansas and the Texas panhandle' / 'panhandle region of Oklahoma' without using the term Anadarko Basin, so they corroborate the GEOGRAPHY but not the specific basin name).

No single citable construction/capital cost found. This is a 97-year-old cumulative asset built and repeatedly expanded/rebuilt across nearly a century (1929 original build, multiple 20th-century mergers, ongoing 21st-century loop/expansion projects under FERC dockets each with their own individual project costs) rather than one discrete project with one publicized total cost -- consistent with the brief's expectation that most SegmentCost units in this batch end UNRESOLVED honestly. Did not force a figure from any single expansion-project cost (e.g. a specific FERC loop docket) since that would misrepresent a component project's cost as the whole system's cost.
